title: Anthropic in the Enterprise — Alexander Bricken & Joe Bayley
talk_summary: An Anthropic applied-AI and GTM talk covering customer case studies (Intercom's Finn) and field best practices: build evals before workflows, define intelligence/cost/latency tradeoffs per use case, and avoid premature fine-tuning.

takeaways.technique: Evals before workflow, evals as IP
takeaways.what_they_do: Design representative eval sets at the start of a use case rather than after building the workflow, and treat the eval set as the durable competitive asset that steers prompt/architecture changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your evals are actually the thing that directs you towards a perfect outcome

takeaways.what_they_do: Include odd/off-distribution inputs (e.g. a kid asking an unrelated question) in eval sets so the model is tested on probable-but-weird traffic, not just happy paths.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you should probably include silly examples like that in your eval set

takeaways.what_they_do: Keep large instruction sets and use prompt caching instead of stripping instructions to save latency, getting big cost and speed wins.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you can just leverage P caching and have a 90% reduction in cost and a 50% increase in speed

takeaways.what_they_do: Improve retrieval so the model gets more relevant context, reducing time spent processing large instruction sets and improving answer quality.
Decide the tradeoff explicitly per use case up front based on stakes and time sensitivity, rather than trying to optimize all three.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the stakes and time sensity sensitivity of the decision should really drive your optimization choices

takeaways.what_they_do: Try prompt engineering, caching, retrieval, and architecture changes first; fine-tuning is costly and can degrade reasoning outside the target domain.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fine tuning is not a silver bullet so it comes at a cost
